problem_motivation.content: There is a lack of research on the oxidation resistance of RHEAs at lower temperatures below 1000 °C, despite their potential for operation in this range.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Much less attention has been paid to the oxidation resistance of RHEAs at lower temperatures.

prior_approach.content: Previous studies examined the oxidation behavior of AlxTiZrNbHfTa RHEAs at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1300 °C.
prior_approach.evidence_span: For instance, an oxidation behavior of a series of Al x TiZrNbHfTa (x = 0–1) RHEAs was examined at temperatures of 700, 900, 1100, and 1300 °C

prior_limitation.content: Prior studies on RHEAs at lower temperatures showed rapid oxidation and disintegration, known as the pesting phenomenon, in specific alloys.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: It was found that at 700 and 900 °C the TiZrNbHfTa alloy exhibited rapid oxidation—the so-called pesting phenomenon. The oxide layer detached easily from the bulk material and the formation of voids on the specimen surface was observed.

prior_limitation.content: Another prior study found that bulk samples of a specific Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy disintegrated into powder after short-term oxidation.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Bulk samples of the alloy disintegrated into powder already after 5 h of oxidation.

prior_limitation.content: The vast majority of existing research on RHEA oxidation was conducted at high temperatures (≥ 1000 °C), leaving a gap for lower temperature data.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Note that the vast majority of the performed research was conducted at temperatures of T ≥ 1000 °C

causal_claim.content: The acceleration of oxidation in the second stage is caused by breakaway oxidation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Most probably, the acceleration of oxidation at the second stage was caused by an effect similar to breakaway oxidation.

mechanism_principle.content: The high strength of the AlNbTiVZr0.25 alloy is caused by strong solid solution strengthening from Zr and the B2 ordered matrix phase.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The high strength of the alloy at ambient and elevated temperatures was attributed to a strong solid solution strengthening induced by Zr and the B2 ordered matrix phase

mechanism_principle.content: The phase stability of the alloy during long-term exposure is due to the presence of Zr, which forms stable phases preventing unwanted transformations.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The reason for the sufficiently high phase stability was the presence of Zr, which prevented any phase transformations due to the formation of its own stable phases, like Zr 5 Al 3 and ZrAlV-type C14 Laves.

mechanism_principle.content: V-rich oxide whiskers indirectly cause cracking by accelerating oxygen ingress and inducing inner nucleation of other oxides.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: it can be speculated that the whisker-like morphology of the V-rich oxides accelerates the ingress of oxygen through the oxide scale, and thereby leads to the Nb 2 O 5 and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides nucleation in its inner part.

mechanism_principle.content: V 2 O 5 evaporation causes pore formation which serves as the primary reason for severe oxidation at 800 °C.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: In addition, the evaporation causes the appearance of multiple pores that serve as places for accelerated ingress of oxygen toward the bare metal and thus stands as the main reason for severe oxidation at 800 °C.

hypothesis_statement.content: The positive effects of Al on oxidation resistance are negated by the presence of V.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Thus, it can be hypothesized that a possible positive effect of Al on the oxidation resistance will be neglected in the presence of V even if Al is added in high amounts.

hypothesis_statement.content: The same oxidation processes observed at 800 °C are responsible for sample disintegration at 900 °C, but occur more rapidly.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: It can be assumed that the same processes, but in a more rapid manner, are responsible for the disintegration of the sample tested at 900 °C.

evidence_result.content: Two-stage oxidation kinetics with nearly parabolic behavior (n = 0.46–0.48) followed by breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) was observed at 600–700 °C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage.

evidence_result.content: The oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing at 800 °C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing.

evidence_result.content: The specimen disintegrated after 50 hours of testing at 900 °C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing.

evidence_result.content: Specific mass gains of 7.2, 38.1, 107.5 mg/cm² at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 225.5 mg/cm² at 900 °C for 50 h were estimated.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively.

evidence_result.content: The surface layer at 600 °C consisted of V2O5, VO2, TiO2, Nb2O5, and TiNb2O7 oxides.
evidence_result.evidence_span: It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V 2 O 5 , VO 2 , TiO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides.

evidence_result.content: The oxide scale at 900 °C comprised complex TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 oxides.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides.

evidence_result.content: The alloy exhibited mixed parabolic-linear oxidation kinetics at 600°C and 700°C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The best fit for 600 °C and 700 °C was found to be mixed parabolic-linear behavior (n = 0.67 for 600 °C, and n = 0.73 for 700 °C)

evidence_result.content: Oxidation kinetics became nearly parabolic at 900°C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The rate of mass gain per unit surface area during oxidation at 900 °C followed a near-parabolic dependence with n = 0.52

evidence_result.content: Oxidation kinetics were rapid and linear-like throughout the duration at 800°C.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 800 °C, a fairly rapid (n = 0.78) oxidation rate was observed throughout the entire duration of testing.

evidence_result.content: The specific mass gain at 900°C led to significant sample disintegration.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Testing at 900 °C was interrupted after 50 h due to the significant disintegration of the sample.

evidence_result.content: At 900°C, the surface layer was composed mainly of complex TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 oxides.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 900 °C, the VO 2 and ZrO 2 oxides were not detected, and the surface layer was comprised mainly of the complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides.

evidence_result.content: Oxidation at 600°C initially occurred heterogeneously with fine oxide nodules.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 600 °C ( Figure 5 a), the oxidation developed heterogeneously, which is evident from the discrepancy in the topographic appearance of different grains. In addition, very fine oxide nodules were found

evidence_result.content: Oxidation at 800°C initially affected all grains homogeneously with oxide whiskers.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At 800 °C ( Figure 5 b), the oxidation affected all the grains homogeneously. The oxide whiskers with the average transversal size of ~500 nm were found at the surface

evidence_result.content: The oxide scale at 600°C contained multiple cracks nucleating at the interface and propagating to the surface.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Multiple cracks in the oxide scale were found; the cracks seemed to nucleate on the scale-metal interface and propagated towards the surface

evidence_result.content: Oxidation front propagation was impeded by the B2 phase but ascended easily along Zr5Al3 particles.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The oxidation front ascended easily along the Zr 5 Al 3 particles but was slightly impeded by the B2 phase.

evidence_result.content: Zr-rich particles dissolved during oxidation, leaving pores at their former sites.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Further, as the oxidation front progressed, Zr-rich particles tended to dissolve with the subsequent formation of the Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxide particles on the borders of their previous location. In addition, a lot of pores were found at the former sites of the Zr-rich particles

evidence_result.content: The specific mass gains for the alloy at 600, 700, and 800 °C were 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5 mg/cm2 respectively.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively.

constraint.content: Oxidation tests were conducted under static lab air conditions.
The accuracy of the analytical balance used for mass measurement is 0.1 mg.

contradiction.content: Contrary to reports that AlNbO4 improves oxidation resistance, the results show it has a detrimental effect in this alloy system.
contradiction.evidence_span: It was reported that the formation of the TiNb 2 O 7 and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides had not improved oxidation resistance, whereas the AlNbO 4 oxide formation resulted in sluggish oxidation kinetics. On the contrary, a number of studies demonstrated the detrimental effect of the AlNbO 4 oxide on the oxidation resistance
